steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Conjugal roles: the roles of husbands and wives within a family. Segregated conjugal roles (Bott): clear division between male (breadwinner) and female (homemaker) roles with separate leisure activities. Joint conjugal roles: couples share tasks and leisure.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Young and Willmott's symmetrical family (1973): the family is becoming more symmetrical - couples share domestic work, decision-making and leisure. They identified three stages: pre-industrial (unit of production), early industrial (segregated roles), symmetrical (joint roles). This change is driven by women working, geographical mobility, and new technology.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Feminist challenge: Oakley (1974) argued the symmetrical family is a myth. Her research found: 72% of husbands had 'no regular domestic duties'; housework and childcare remain overwhelmingly done by women; men may do more visible tasks (DIY, driving) but not routine daily work. The British Social Attitudes survey (2018) shows women still do twice as much housework as men.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The impact of women working: dual-earner families are now the norm (72% of women work). This has increased women's financial independence and bargaining power in the home. However, working women still do most housework - Ferri and Smith called this the 'dual burden' (paid work plus unpaid housework).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe Young and Willmott's symmetrical family and evaluate whether it accurately represents modern family life. | Explain how feminism has challenged traditional family roles, using evidence. | Evaluate whether conjugal roles have become more equal in modern families.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Young and Willmott: roles becoming SYMMETRICAL (equal). Oakley: this is a MYTH - women still do most housework. Dual burden = paid work + housework. Triple shift = paid work + housework + emotional work. Progress is incomplete: women work more but still do most domestic labour. Public equality > domestic equality.
